newsitem.title: UK: Britain sets up inquiry into deaths in custody.
newsitem.headline: Britain sets up inquiry into deaths in custody.

text.p: England's director of public prosecutions ordered an urgent inquiry on Friday into the handling of serious complaints about police handling of prisoners in custody, including two deaths.

Barbara Mills, the head of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) which is responsible for prosecuting criminal cases, decided to investigate her own department after judges overturned two CPS rulings not to prosecute police officers in connection with two deaths in custody.

"The DPP has set up an urgent inquiry into the decision-making process within the CPS...and if necessary beyond, following the findings of the Divisional Court this week that there may have been a weakness in the way decisions not to prosecute were taken," a CPS spokesman said in a statement.

Mills had come under pressure to resign after the court overturned CPS decisions in the case of an Irish-born man who died of suffocation while in police custody and a Nigerian who also died while under arrest.
Deborah Coles, the director of Inquest, a pressure group that monitors deaths in police custody, said Mills's position was untenable following the court rulings.
"These cases have exposed real serious problems in that department that have to be addressed at the highest level," she told BBC radio.
The two cases involved in the decision concern Richard O'Brien, a father of seven, and Shiji Lapite, a Nigerian who was seeking asylum in Britain. Their wives fought to have the cases reviewed.

The CPS, which handles the most serious cases in the country and is staffed by about 60 lawyers and 100 caseworkers, said the independent inquiry will report to Mills and the findings will be made public.
